source.title: Strong inductive biases provably prevent harmless interpolation
source.authors: Michael Aerni; Marco Milanta; Konstantin Donhauser; Fanny Yang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses double descent and argues that its own inductive-bias results are distinct from it. Its experiments vary inductive bias and compare interpolation with early stopping; they do not test the claim’s size-, epoch-, or sample-wise double-descent curves.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results on harmful versus harmless interpolation as inductive bias changes, but does not measure the claim’s double-descent curves. Those results are recorded as findings that fit no listed version. No results cited from other work are included. Hyperparameter choices and loss values used to motivate setup are not recorded as claim results.
record.test_reason: The paper studies whether interpolating noisy data is harmless as inductive-bias strength varies (filter size, rotational invariance), in kernel regression theory and in CNN/WRN experiments. It discusses double descent only to argue its phenomenon is distinct (Sec. 4.1, App. E.3). Its width-scaling checks keep models well past the interpolation threshold. It reports no test-error curve over model size, epochs or samples through a threshold, and no peak location or peak removal. No listed version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that strong inductive biases make interpolating noisy data harmful. Weak biases make interpolation harmless and even require fitting some noise. They explain this as a bias-variance trade-off and argue, using width-scaling experiments, that it is distinct from double descent.
record.recipe_differences: The paper studies convolutional-kernel and neural-network interpolation while varying structural inductive bias, and compares interpolating estimators with optimally regularized or early-stopped ones. It does not reproduce the original model-size, epoch, or sample-size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported interpolation gap changes with CNN filter size and with the number of augmented rotations; it also varies with label noise and inductive-bias strength. The paper reports that the qualitative behavior persists when network width is increased.

fits_no_version.finding: In convolutional-kernel regression, interpolation is harmful relative to optimal ridge for strong inductive bias (β<β*) and harmless for weak bias (β>β*).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether interpolating noisy data is harmless depends on the strength of structural inductive bias.

fits_no_version.finding: For the min-norm interpolator, bias falls as the inductive bias strengthens, while variance shows a multiple-descent curve in β.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Varying structural inductive bias produces a bias-variance trade-off, with multiple descent in variance.

fits_no_version.finding: In synthetic-image CNNs with 20% noise, the gap between interpolating and early-stopped test error grows as filter size shrinks. Optimally stopped small-filter models fit none of the noisy samples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Structural bias governs both the cost of interpolation and how much noise optimal early stopping fits.

fits_no_version.finding: In WRNs on EuroSAT, more rotational-invariance augmentation enlarges the interpolation gap under 20% noise. Without invariance, optimal stopping fits some noise.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Invariance strength affects the cost of interpolation and noise fitting.

fits_no_version.finding: At filter size 5, the gap between interpolating and early-stopped test error persists at widths 1024 and 2048.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Increasing width does not remove the cost of interpolation under strong structural bias.

record.problems: Main experimental curves are figures without tabulated point values. The synthetic-image experiments use five dataset draws; the EuroSAT experiments use one sampled dataset and five training seeds. Optimal early stopping is selected using the test error, as the authors state.
record.rows_left_out: No claim-bearing results were left out. The appendix reports additional width and rotation experiments mainly in figures; only the numeric width-1024 and width-2048 results in Table 1 are included. Figure 5 training-loss comparisons are not results on the claim’s behavior and are omitted.

untested.parts: No sweep of model size through the interpolation threshold. The width checks (128 to 2048 filters; WRN widen factor 6 to 12) stay deliberately far past the threshold.
Test error over epochs is used only to pick the oracle early-stopping point; no epoch-wise curve shape is reported.
No capacity-risk curve across model classes.
No effective-complexity measure is used to predict peak locations.

Label noise and optimal ridge/early stopping are varied, but not with respect to a double-descent peak. The multiple descent reported is of variance against filter-size exponent β, not of test error across capacity.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T6/discusses classification holds. The paper's double-descent argument concerns its own phenomenon, not evidence that a version is wrong, so it is not T5. The Figure 6/7 width sweeps are declared in rows_left_out and stay past the threshold. The Table 1 percent units should be checked.

versions.untested_parts: No test-error sweep over model size or interpolation threshold.
No test-error curve over epochs or training time.
No sweep over the number of training samples near an interpolation threshold.
No capacity-risk curves across model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is evaluated as predicting peak locations.

The paper varies label noise and compares interpolation with optimal regularization/early stopping, and reports multiple descent of variance versus inductive-bias strength. It does not test whether a double-descent peak is driven by noise, whether that peak splits, or whether optimally tuned regularization removes such a peak.
No re-counting of complexity by effective parameters or test of whether that turns a second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: kernel ridge regression with cyclic convolutional kernels
rows.operation_detail: Varied filter-size growth rate β and compared the min-RKHS-norm interpolator with the optimally ridge-regularized estimator.
rows.measure: Population risk of interpolation relative to optimal ridge regularization
rows.baseline: Optimally ridge-regularized estimator has strictly better risk rates than the interpolator.
rows.value: Interpolation is harmful; the regularized estimator’s rates are strictly better.
rows.uncertainty: not stated
rows.note: The outcome concerns inductive-bias strength, not risk over model size, epochs, or sample size.

rows.subject: kernel ridge regression with cyclic convolutional kernels
rows.operation_detail: Varied filter-size growth rate β and compared the min-RKHS-norm interpolator with the optimally ridge-regularized estimator.

rows.baseline: Optimally ridge-regularized estimator has the same risk rates as the interpolator.
rows.value: Interpolation is harmless; the two estimators’ rates match.
rows.uncertainty: not stated
rows.note: This is a comparison across inductive-bias strengths, not a double-descent curve.

rows.subject: min-RKHS-norm interpolator with cyclic convolutional kernel
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed bias and variance rates as the filter-size growth rate β changes.

rows.uncertainty: not stated
rows.note: The reported multiple descent is variance against filter-size growth rate, not test error against model size, epochs, or sample size.
